question: Why do tablets or injections (systemic drugs) often struggle to treat eye problems effectively?

options.A: Blood vessels in the eye destroy active ingredients
options.B: Unique barriers like the cornea block them from getting inside
options.C: Systemic drugs cannot dissolve in body fluids
options.D: The liver breaks down all eye medications too quickly

explanation: Think of the eye as a well-guarded fort! Natural barriers like the cornea make it hard for drugs travelling through your bloodstream to get inside the eye in strong enough amounts.

question: What is the main benefit of giving medications directly as eye or ear drops instead of pills?

options.A: It stops the patient from blinking too much during the day
options.B: It completely removes the need for nursing assessments
options.C: It keeps the drug working locally and prevents unwanted body-wide side effects
options.D: It ensures the drug goes straight to the liver for activation

explanation: Spot-on! Using drops means the medicine stays right where it's needed in the eye or ear, without floating all around the rest of the body causing side effects.

question: What is the main goal of using medicine for glaucoma?

options.A: To lower pressure inside the eye and protect the optic nerve
options.B: To increase blood flow directly to the retina and lens
options.C: To cure bacterial infections in the cornea
options.D: To widen the pupil and improve night vision

explanation: You've got this! In glaucoma, fluid builds up and creates pressure. Our main goal is to relieve that pressure so the delicate optic nerve stays safe from damage.

question: A patient is given timolol eye drops for glaucoma. How do these drops actually lower eye pressure?

options.A: By dissolving protein deposits on the clear cornea
options.B: By widening the tear drainage system
options.C: By completely relaxing the outer eye muscles
options.D: By decreasing the production of fluid (aqueous humor)

explanation: Timolol is a beta-blocker. It tells the ciliary body to slow down on making fluid (aqueous humor), which lowers the pressure inside the eye. Neat, right?

question: What does a 'cycloplegic' drug do when dropped into the eye?

options.A: Increases the drainage of fluid from the eye chambers
options.B: Constricts the pupil down to a tiny pinpoint size
options.C: Numbs the surface of the cornea for a quick check
options.D: Paralyzes the focusing muscle inside the eye

explanation: Cycloplegics put the ciliary muscle on pause so it can't focus. This is super helpful during eye exams or surgeries when the eye needs to stay completely relaxed.

question: Why should a nurse remind patients using mydriatic (pupil-dilating) drops to wear sunglasses outside?

options.A: The medication changes the natural color of the iris
options.B: Bright sunlight can make the cornea swell up rapidly
options.C: Ultraviolet rays will destroy the active drug
options.D: Their widened pupils let in way too much glaring light

explanation: When pupils are forced wide open by drops, they can't shrink down to block bright sunlight. Sunglasses save the patient from painful glare!

question: Which problem is most linked to using steroid eye drops for a very long time?

options.B: Secondary glaucoma and increased eye pressure
options.C: Rapid hardening of the outer eye layer
options.D: Permanent pupil shrinkage and total blindness

explanation: Steroids are great for short-term inflammation, but long-term use can block fluid drainage and shoot pressure right up, leading to secondary glaucoma.

question: Why must a nurse check for a germ or fungus infection before giving a strong steroid eye drop?

options.A: Viral infections always require heavy systemic steroids
options.B: Antifungal drugs neutralize the active ingredients in steroids
options.C: Steroid drops only work if mixed with an antibiotic first
options.D: Steroids weaken the local immune response and can make infections spread

explanation: Steroids calm down inflammation by putting the brakes on the immune system. If a hidden fungus or virus is present, that brake-action lets the germ throw a party and spread!

question: What is the main reason nurses use fluorescein sodium eye drops?

options.A: To dilate the pupil for a deep retinal view
options.B: To kill bacteria causing severe pink eye
options.C: To highlight scratches and foreign objects on the cornea under special light
options.D: To numb the surface before checking eye pressure

explanation: Fluorescein is a brilliant diagnostic tool! It clings to damaged spots on the cornea and glows bright green under a blue light so you can easily spot tiny scratches.

question: Why is it dangerous for a patient to rub their eye right after getting a numbing (anesthetic) drop?

options.A: Rubbing forces the medication deep into the tear ducts
options.B: Friction triggers an immediate severe allergy
options.C: Pressure changes will rupture internal blood vessels
options.D: They can scratch their cornea without feeling the pain

explanation: Numbing drops take away pain sensation temporarily. If the patient rubs their eye hard, they could easily scratch the delicate tissue and won't even feel it happening!

question: What is the job of a cerumenolytic drug like carbamide peroxide?

options.A: To numb the ear canal before minor procedures
options.B: To kill bacteria causing deep ear infections
options.C: To soften and break down hard earwax for easy removal
options.D: To dry up fluid draining from the eardrum

explanation: Cerumenolytics do exactly what their name suggests: they break down stubborn, impacted earwax so it's a breeze to clear out of the canal.

question: Why should ear drops (otic drops) always be warmed to room temperature before putting them in?

options.B: Cold drops can instantly burst the eardrum
options.C: Cold medication is too thick to pass through the ear canal
options.D: Cold drops can shock the inner ear and cause severe dizziness

explanation: Putting ice-cold drops straight into the ear canal tickles the balance center in the inner ear the wrong way, triggering sudden vertigo and nausea. Always warm them in your hands first!

question: When giving ear drops to an adult patient, how should you pull the outer ear (pinna)?
explanation: A classic clinical tip! For adults, pulling the pinna up and back straightens out the wiggly ear canal so the drops flow smoothly all the way down.

question: After putting glaucoma eye drops in a patient, what quick action stops the medicine from entering the rest of the body?

options.A: Wipe the outer eyelids firmly with an alcohol swab
options.B: Tell the patient to blink rapidly twenty times
options.C: Cover both eyes with a thick pressure bandage
options.D: Apply gentle pressure to the inner corner near the tear duct

explanation: Gentle pressure on the inner corner (nasolacrimal occlusion) blocks the drop from draining down into the nose and entering the bloodstream. Smart nursing care!

question: Why is patient teaching so important when managing chronic open-angle glaucoma?

options.A: Patients have to perform mini-surgeries at home
options.B: Eye drops must be mixed with clean water before every use
options.C: The disease is usually painless, so patients might skip lifelong treatment
options.D: The medications cure the underlying nerve damage quickly

explanation: Because chronic glaucoma doesn't hurt, patients often feel totally fine and forget to take their daily drops. Good teaching helps them see why consistency is life-saving for their vision.

question: Which of these is NOT a safe way to source or store eye medications in a resource-limited setting?

options.A: Buying products only from verified, licensed pharmacies
options.B: Keeping drops away from direct sun and heavy heat
options.C: Buying medications from roadside hawkers to save money
options.D: Checking the expiry date before every application

explanation: Never buy drugs from roadside vendors! They often sell fake, expired, or poorly stored medications that can ruin vision or cause dangerous eye infections.
